tasks.locator: Methods › Study Selection; Results › Literature Search; Results › Study Characteristics
tasks.extracted: Registered review (PROSPERO CRD42017059224): 22 studies (10 prospective cohort, 12 cross-sectional) out of 73 candidate articles; 3 rated high risk of bias. Five databases, 1 January 1973 to 30 April 2018, English only; people older than 12 years with at least 30 days of lifetime cannabis use. 13 distinct outcomes, 5 poolable. Every exposure described is smoking (joints, joint-years); methods of quantifying use varied (monthly, weekly or daily use; joint-years; cigarette-years).

tasks.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend
tasks.extracted: Prospective cohorts, 2 studies pooled (Dunedin cohort, n = 1037, mean follow-up 15 years, use about once a week for a year on average; Los Angeles cohort, 299 people, mean 3.0 joints a day for 9.8 years, 49% lost to follow-up), people who used cannabis against people who did not: cough RR 2.04 (95% CI 1.02 to 4.06), RD 0.07 (0.02 to 0.13); sputum production RR 3.84 (1.62 to 9.07), RD 0.12 (-0.02 to 0.25); heterogeneity low. After the Knapp-Hartung adjustment the pooled RRs were not significant (cough P = 0.10; sputum P = 0.20). Both studies found that stopping cannabis was followed by a significant fall in respiratory symptoms. The abstract and Results report the pooled intervals (which exclude 1) as showing an increased risk; the Figure 2 legend gives the Knapp-Hartung P values.

tasks.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Single prospective studies not pooled: the Tucson random-sample cohort (n = 1802, four surveys 1981 to 1988, moderate risk of bias) found current cannabis smoking associated with chronic cough OR 1.73 (1.21 to 2.47), chronic sputum OR 1.53 (1.08 to 2.18) and wheezing OR 2.01 (1.50 to 2.70); the Dunedin study found wheezing OR 1.55 (1.23 to 1.94), P < 0.001, and a trend for dyspnea OR 1.23 (0.97 to 1.56), P = 0.086.

tasks.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 legend; Table (wheezing comment); Discussion, 5th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Cross-sectional studies, 4 pooled (1 low and 3 moderate risk of bias; all included moderate to heavy use), people who used cannabis against people who did not: cough RR 4.37 (1.71 to 11.19), RD 0.18 (0.15 to 0.21); sputum production RR 3.40 (1.99 to 5.79), RD 0.14 (0.10 to 0.17); wheezing RR 2.83 (1.89 to 4.23), RD 0.22 (0.14 to 0.29); dyspnea RR 1.56 (1.33 to 1.83), RD 0.06 (-0.01 to 0.13). Knapp-Hartung P: cough 0.05, sputum 0.05, wheezing 0.01, dyspnea below 0.01. Heterogeneity was high for wheezing and is attributed to non-uniform exposure and symptom definitions. The pooled risk differences are weighted differently from the ratios (for dyspnea the ratio's interval excludes 1 while the difference's includes 0) and mostly reflect one or two large studies, so they are not typical figures; which four studies were pooled is shown only in a forest-plot image, which was not read.

tasks.locator: Results › Obstructive Lung Disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 3 legend
tasks.extracted: Chronic bronchitis and COPD: the Los Angeles cohort (3.0 joints a day, mean 9.8 years, 49% lost) found more bronchitis episodes, OR 2.3 (1.2 to 4.4), P = 0.011. Three cross-sectional studies pooled: RR 2.28 (0.68 to 7.72), RD 0.06 (-0.04 to 0.16), not significant (Knapp-Hartung P = 0.31). SPIROMICS (n = 1174, people currently or formerly smoking tobacco only): current use OR 0.87 (0.59 to 1.31), former use OR 1.0 (0.79 to 1.26). A high-risk-of-bias study found COPD prevalence higher by 0.3% (0.0% to 0.5%) per joint-year, with people who used cannabis and tobacco combined.

tasks.locator: Results › Change in Pulmonary Function › FEV1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; FVC, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: FEV1: CARDIA (rated low risk of bias; 5115 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start): current use, adjusted mean difference −18 mL (−42 to 6.1); a Los Angeles cohort (mean age 33, over 3.5 joints a day, 8 years): no significant fall in people who smoked cannabis continuously or intermittently against people who did not smoke it; Dunedin (10 years): no change. FVC: CARDIA lifetime use over 10 joint-years +59 mL (12 to 107); cross-sectional SPIROMICS higher FVC in current and former use and NHANES +0.07% per joint-year (NHANES and SPIROMICS reported FEV1 only for cannabis and tobacco smoking combined). The review describes the CARDIA −18 mL as minimal exposure and attaches trend P values (0.32, 0.03, 0.01) to single contrasts; in the primary paper the −18 mL contrast is the heaviest current category and those P values are for trend, so CARDIA is cited from the primary paper (anchors below).

tasks.locator: Results › Change in Pulmonary Function › FEV1, 2nd paragraph; FEV1-FVC Ratio, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › Airway Resistance and Specific Conductance of Airways
tasks.extracted: Tucson (4 to 5 cannabis cigarettes a week, moderate risk of bias): significant FEV1 reductions after 1 year (P < 0.01) and a significant reduction in the FEV1-FVC ratio. NHANES 2007 to 2010 (low risk of bias): more than 20 joint-years against people who did not smoke cannabis, ratio below 70%, OR 2.1 (1.1 to 3.9) after tobacco adjustment (the earlier NHANES study, moderate risk of bias: no definite relationship); SPIROMICS (mean 30.1 joint-years, all with a tobacco-smoking history): positive association with a low ratio, P < 0.001; a Wellington study (n = 339, mean 54.2 joint-years) marginally lower ratio, −1.1% (−2.6% to 0.1%). All four studies of airway resistance and specific conductance (1 prospective, low risk of bias; 3 cross-sectional) found higher resistance and lower conductance in people who smoked cannabis.

tasks.locator: Results › Strength of Evidence; Table
tasks.extracted: Strength of evidence (AHRQ method): low for cough, sputum production, wheezing and airway resistance; insufficient for dyspnea, obstructive lung disease, FEV1, FVC, FEV1-FVC ratio and other respiratory outcomes.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Results › Study Characteristics
tasks.extracted: The authors say the lung-function evidence is limited by low exposure and young cohorts: tobacco's effect on FEV1 becomes measurable only after about 5 to 10 pack-years; obstructive lung disease develops in about a third of people who smoke tobacco long term and is usually identified after age 35 to 40; large cohorts of middle-aged to older people with heavier cannabis exposure may be needed. They add, as a conjecture, that few people may use enough cannabis to change lung function, so lung function may not be among its most important long-term health outcomes. Across all prospective lung-function evaluations only 243 people (131 cannabis-only) had more than 20 joint-years; the authors also count 756 people who smoked cannabis only with more than 20 joint-years across all outcomes and studies (a different scope).

tasks.locator: Methods › Study Design and Sample; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1; Abstract (Results)
tasks.extracted: 5115 adults aged 18 to 30 were recruited in 1985 to 1986 in four US cities; spirometry at years 0, 2, 5, 10 and 20 with 69% retention at year 20. Of 20,777 visits with spirometry, 19,703 (95%) from 5016 participants (98%) were used, 3.9 visits each on average; attrition was more common in people who smoked tobacco and not associated with cannabis use. 54% reported current cannabis or tobacco smoking, or both, at one or more exams (neither 2305, tobacco only 851, cannabis only 795, both 1065). Cannabis exposure was nearly as common as tobacco but mostly light: median 2 to 3 episodes in the past 30 days against 8 to 9 cigarettes a day for tobacco; 91 participants had no tobacco exposure and more than 10 joint-years of cannabis (153 spirometry observations), 40 of them more than 20 joint-years (56 observations).

tasks.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: One model with all four smoking variables (current and lifetime cannabis and tobacco). Cannabis, four-level categories, tobacco in the same model: lifetime exposure was associated with higher FVC and FEV1 than zero exposure (1 to 5 joint-years FEV1 +38 mL, 15 to 62; FVC +41 mL, 14 to 67; 6 to 10 joint-years FEV1 +66 mL, 32 to 100; FVC +54 mL, 16 to 91; over 10 joint-years FEV1 +36 mL, -6.5 to 79; FVC +59 mL, 12 to 107). Current heavy use (over 20 episodes in the past 30 days) was FEV1 -18 mL (-42 to 6.1) and FVC +20 mL (-5.2 to 49); people who used cannabis only differed little from people using neither (FEV1 +0.7 mL, -12 to 13; FVC +8.2 mL, -5 to 22), while tobacco only was -24 mL (-38 to -11) for FEV1. The Results text gives the top lifetime category as 'more than 20' joint-years while Table 2 labels it 'more than 10'; Table 2's label is used.

tasks.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 3 (lifetime marijuana rows); Abstract (Results)
tasks.extracted: Cannabis, spline models: the association with lifetime exposure was non-linear (P < 0.001 for FEV1 and FVC). The slope was +13 mL per joint-year for FEV1 (6.4 to 20) and +20 mL for FVC (12 to 27) at 2 joint-years, about zero at 7 joint-years (FEV1 -0.4, -2.6 to 1.8; FVC 0.0, -2.4 to 2.5), and for FEV1 -2.2 mL per joint-year (-4.6 to 0.3, P = 0.079) at 20 and 50 joint-years. Net FEV1 difference against no exposure: +53 mL (28 to 79) at 7 joint-years, +27 mL (-10 to 64) at 20 and -39 mL (-141 to 64) at 50; net FVC +64 (36 to 92), +76 (34 to 117) and +104 (-12 to 220). The Results text gives the interval of the −2.2 slope as −4.9 to 0.36 against −4.6 to 0.3 in the abstract and Table 3; neither is significant.

tasks.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 3 (current marijuana rows)
tasks.extracted: Current intensity, spline models: non-linear for both outcomes (FEV1 P = 0.025, FVC P = 0.035). At 20 episodes a month the FEV1 slope was -3.2 mL per episode a month (-5.8 to -0.6, P = 0.017) and the FVC slope -1.5 (-4.2 to 1.3); net differences at 20 episodes a month were FEV1 +14 mL (-4.7 to 32) and FVC +43 mL (23 to 63). No data at 40 episodes a month. The authors state the net FEV1 association became negative only at very high exposure (over 40 joint-years or 25 episodes a month) and not significantly.

tasks.locator: Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2; Table 3 (lifetime tobacco rows)
tasks.extracted: Tobacco (positive control): current smoking of more than 20 cigarettes a day was associated with FEV1 63 mL lower (95% CI -89 to -36) and FVC 69 mL lower (-97 to -41); lifetime exposure over 20 pack-years with FEV1 101 mL lower (-136 to -65). In spline models the association was linear and dose-related, with a slope of -7.0 mL per pack-year (-10 to -3.7) at 7 pack-years and net differences at 50 pack-years of -332 mL (-401 to -263) for FEV1 and -229 mL (-310 to -147) for FVC. No statistically significant interaction between tobacco and cannabis exposure was found for FEV1 or FVC.

tasks.locator: Comment, 1st paragraph; Comment, 6th to 8th paragraphs; final paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors conclude that up to about 7 joint-years of lifetime exposure (for example 1 joint a day for 7 years or 1 joint a week for 49 years) gave no evidence that more exposure harms lung function, that at higher exposure the pattern levelled off or reversed especially for FEV1, and that the sample contained too few people with heavy use to confirm a harmful effect of very heavy use. They propose a stretch or training effect (one version called a speculative possibility) and a short-lived airway widening, which they consider unlikely to explain the higher volumes. Limitations named by the authors: no plethysmography, diffusing capacity or imaging of emphysema; only a minority with very high cannabis exposure, fewer still without tobacco, so estimates at high exposure are imprecise; self-reported exposure with recall error and no record of smoking method; unmeasured confounding possible. The final paragraph says the findings suggest an accelerated decline with heavy use, but the net FEV1 differences at 20 and 50 joint-years and the spline slope (−2.2 mL per joint-year, P = 0.079) were not significant; only the slope for current use at 20 episodes a month was (−3.2 mL per episode a month, P = 0.017).

tasks.locator: Results › Cohort derivation, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Methods › Data sources; Discussion, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Of 35,114 Ontario residents aged 12 to 65 in the CCHS who either used cannabis in the past year or were controls, 6425 (18.3%) used cannabis in the past year; 4807 of them (74.8%) were matched to 10,395 controls (15,202 people). After matching, 73.9% of both groups currently or formerly smoked tobacco and standardised differences were below 0.10 for all variables. Cannabis use frequency in the matched cannabis group: less than once a month 42.5%, 1 to 3 times a month 18.1%, once a week 9.4%, more than once a week 11.4%, every day 10.5%, unknown 8.0%. Route, amount and potency were not collected; the authors say inhalation is by far the most common route (citing a scoping review).

tasks.locator: Results › Overall cohort analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Primary outcome, respiratory-related ER visit or hospital admission within 12 months: 175 events (3.6%) in the cannabis group against 410 (3.9%) in controls, OR 0.91 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.09), p = 0.32. All-cause ER visit or admission: 1443 (30.0%) against 2699 (26.0%), OR 1.22 (1.13 to 1.31), number needed to harm 25. All-cause death: 11 against 24 (0.2% each), OR 0.99 (0.49 to 2.02).

tasks.locator: Results › Sensitivity analyses › By sex; By tobacco smoking history; By pre-existing asthma or COPD; Table 4
tasks.extracted: Respiratory outcome by tobacco history: people currently or formerly smoking tobacco OR 0.80 (0.65 to 0.99), p = 0.04 (123 events, 3.5%, against 290, 4.2%); people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record OR 1.23 (0.89 to 1.70). All-cause outcome: 1.16 (1.06 to 1.26) and 1.35 (1.16 to 1.56). By sex, respiratory OR 1.00 (0.77 to 1.31) in men and 0.86 (0.68 to 1.10) in women; by pre-existing asthma or COPD, respiratory OR 0.82 (0.61 to 1.11) with and 0.96 (0.77 to 1.20) without. One row of Table 4 is internally inconsistent (events in the cannabis group 149 + 33 = 182, not the 175 of Table 2); people with missing tobacco status are analysed with people who never smoked tobacco.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st and 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors give reasons the null respiratory result may understate an effect (not adjustable): too little cannabis smoke exposure among people in the study (citing research that lung-function decline occurs only above 20 'joints per year'), some non-inhaled use, secondhand cannabis smoke in controls, and low power. They also say the large share of people in the cannabis group who used it infrequently may have contributed to the null result, that causation should not be inferred, and that unmeasured confounding might explain the positive findings. Limitations stated: self-report (recall and social-desirability bias); no dose-response (frequency categories too small); no quantity or potency data; about 25% of the cannabis group unmatched; data only before October 2018; no secondhand-smoke adjustment; too few people under 20 and aged 50 to 65 for age-group analyses; a single province. The Discussion's threshold of 20 joints per year for lung-function decline is the wrong unit (CARDIA uses joint-years) and a threshold the cited cohort did not establish.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7 › Respiratory Symptoms, Including Chronic Bronchitis › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Hancox 2015, Walden and Earleywine, Tashkin 2012); Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Conclusion 7-3
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Respiratory symptoms (Conclusion 7-3): the committee graded as substantial the evidence of a statistical association (7-3a) between long-term cannabis smoking and worse respiratory symptoms and more frequent chronic bronchitis episodes, and as moderate the evidence of an association (7-3b) between stopping and improvement. Under it: a 2007 systematic review of 14 symptom studies (nine cross-sectional, three case series, one case-control, one cohort; cough OR 1.7 to 2.0, sputum 1.5 to 1.9, wheeze 2.0 to 3.0); the Wellington cross-sectional study (cough 29% against 5%, wheeze 27% against 11%, chronic bronchitis symptoms 19% against 3%, people who smoked cannabis against people who did not); the Dunedin cohort of 1,037 followed to age 38 (frequent use, defined as 52 or more times in the past year: morning cough OR 1.97, sputum 2.31, wheeze 1.55; fewer symptoms after quitting); an internet survey of 5,987 adults recruited through drug-policy-reform organisations; a longitudinal cohort of 299 followed for at least two visits over 9.8 years, with high or variable loss to follow-up (current against never use: cough OR 1.7, sputum 2.1, bronchitis episodes 2.3, wheeze 3.4; current against former use: cough 3.3, sputum 4.2, wheeze 2.1). The committee notes no clear additive effect of smoking both cannabis and tobacco on symptoms.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7 › Respiratory Symptoms › Primary Studies (paragraphs after Figure 7-1 on Hancox 2015 limitations and on Walden and Earleywine); Discussion of Findings, 2nd paragraph
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Limits of the symptom evidence as the committee states them: most studies relied on self-reported cannabis smoking; many did not control for tobacco and occupational or environmental exposures, or for dose or duration; joint-years were rarely used and the THC content of a joint varies widely between joints and between years; Dunedin classed fewer than 52 uses a year as non-use and did not know whether cannabis was smoked; the internet survey recruited through organisations advocating drug-policy reform.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7 › Pulmonary Function › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Papatheodorou, Pletcher, Hancox 2010, Van Dam and Earleywine); Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-1; Chapter Highlights
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Lung function (Conclusion 7-1): 'moderate evidence' of an association between cannabis smoking and improved airway dynamics with acute use but not chronic use (7-1a) and with higher FVC (7-1b); the chapter highlight says it is unclear whether cannabis use is associated with worsened lung function. Under it: the 2007 review (34 publications; acute bronchodilation; regular smoking associated with lower specific airway conductance, about 16% on average, and a lower FEV1; inconsistent findings otherwise); CARDIA, 5,115 adults over 20 years, occasional and low cumulative smoking not associated with adverse effects on lung function, with a trend to lower FEV1 only at the heaviest exposure (20 or more joint-years) and with few people at heavy exposure; Dunedin (1,037, spirometry at 32): cumulative cannabis associated with higher FVC, total lung capacity and residual volume but not lower FEV1 or FEV1/FVC; NHANES 2007 to 2012 (10,327 adults, cross-sectional): lower FEV1/FVC and higher FEV1 and FVC in people who had smoked cannabis recently; a 12-person vaporizer feasibility study with no control group.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7 › Pulmonary Function › Primary Studies, paragraph on Aldington et al. (2007)
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Wellington sample (Aldington et al., 2007; convenience sample of 339; entry required at least 5 joint-years of cannabis or 1 pack-year of tobacco, according to what was smoked; self-reported use): no association between long-term cannabis smoking and the lung-function variables in the main analysis, but per joint-year a significantly lower FEV1/FVC, lower specific airways conductance and higher total lung capacity than in people who did not smoke; the authors estimated that each joint's association with a lower FEV1/FVC was similar to that of 2.5 to 5 tobacco cigarettes. The committee criticises the analysis: only main effects were reported (no test of interaction between cannabis and tobacco) and coefficients were labelled odds ratios in two tables. The committee cites the same paper for the symptom percentages.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7 › Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Tan 2009, Yadavilli, Macleod, Kempker); Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-2
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: COPD (Conclusion 7-2): 'limited evidence' of an association between occasional cannabis smoking and developing COPD when controlled for tobacco (7-2a); 'insufficient evidence' for hospital admissions for COPD (7-2b). Under it: a 339-person Wellington CT study with inconsistent results; Vancouver cross-sectional study of 878 adults (at least 50 cannabis cigarettes and no tobacco history: not at significantly greater risk of COPD or more respiratory symptoms; tobacco plus cannabis not clearly different from tobacco only); a 709-person readmission study (cannabis 0.22 against tobacco 0.26, unit not specified); a 500-person cross-sectional study with no non-smoking group (COPD 24.3% tobacco only against 25.2% tobacco plus cannabis, p = 0.90; more cough, phlegm and wheeze with both, no adjusted comparison); NHANES (more than 20 joint-years, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.1 to 3.9, but higher FVC and no FEV1 association, and pre-bronchodilator spirometry). The Discussion says it is unclear whether regular use is associated with developing or worsening COPD and cites a position statement of minimal impairment in people who smoke cannabis occasionally once tobacco is controlled for. The basis for the word occasional in Conclusion 7-2(a) is not apparent in the text read: the studies described do not show an association in people who smoke cannabis occasionally.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7 › Asthma › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies; Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-4
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Asthma (Conclusion 7-4): no or insufficient evidence to support or refute an association between cannabis smoking and asthma development or exacerbation, from a 506-boy cohort that found no link to self-reported asthma symptoms, a cohort of 110 adolescents with asthma that found no association with asthma concern, severity or symptoms, and one case-control letter of 100 emergency department patients that found no association with THC. The Discussion adds that wheeze appears common among people who use cannabis.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7 › Respiratory Symptoms › Primary Studies, paragraph on Van Dam and Earleywine; Pulmonary Function › Primary Studies, paragraph on Van Dam and Earleywine; Respiratory Symptoms › Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Research Gaps
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Van Dam and Earleywine (2010), as the committee describes it: 12 adults; switching from smoking cannabis to a vaporizer was correlated with resolution of cannabis-related respiratory symptoms, and with improved forced expiratory volumes, about 1 month later; no control group. The committee lists as unknown whether other inhaled forms of cannabis cause fewer respiratory symptoms and asks for trials of them against smoking.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7 › Summary, 1st paragraph; Research Gaps, 1st paragraph and bullets
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Chapter 7 Summary and gaps: the committee judges the respiratory risks of cannabis smoking to be relatively small and well below those of tobacco smoking; it says people who smoke heavily may be at higher risk of chronic bronchitis and COPD but that current studies do not give enough evidence of a link; and it names the limitations (cannabis and tobacco hard to separate; self-reported exposure; few cohorts of people who smoke regularly or daily; inadequate control of environmental factors; generalisability). Unknown, it says: whether long-term cannabis smoking above tobacco causes faster lung-function decline, chronic bronchitis or COPD; whether it raises the risk of allergic disease or asthma; whether other inhaled forms cause fewer respiratory symptoms. The tobacco comparison is the committee's overall judgment in the Summary, not a numbered conclusion; the chapter holds pieces pointing both ways and the sections read give no study comparing the two at matched exposure.
tasks.quote: appear to be relatively small and to be far lower than those of tobacco smoking

tasks.locator: Chapter 7 › opening text (before Pulmonary Function), 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Background given for smoke exposure: in 15 volunteers one cannabis joint gave about four times the carbon monoxide exposure and three to five times the tar deposition of a single cigarette, with deeper inhalation, longer breath-holding and no filters; against this, cannabis cigarettes are less densely packed and people who use cannabis usually smoke fewer of them per day than people who smoke tobacco smoke cigarettes.

tasks.locator: Appendix B › Data Synthesis and Strength of Evidence Assessment, 1st paragraph; Box B-3; Chapter 7 › Chapter Highlights
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Method, wording of conclusions: evidence was privileged in the order randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies, case-control studies, with case series only when nothing better; the committee notes that this order does not imply the size of an observed effect. The weight of evidence was decided in private deliberations of committee subgroups. Box B-3 defines substantial (several supportive findings from good-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings), moderate (several from good- to fair-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings; limitations including chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out), limited (fair-quality studies or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion; significant uncertainty) and no or insufficient (mixed findings, a single poor study, or not studied). The Chapter 7 highlight predicts that stopping will probably reduce chronic cough and phlegm, causal wording over Conclusion 7-3(b), which grades only an association from cohorts with loss to follow-up. Appendix B does not place cross-sectional studies, the commonest design in Chapter 7, in its order of evidence.

tasks.locator: An Urgent Call for Change in Cannabis Research › Complications of cannabis research, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Tobacco and other co-occurring use: about 70% of people who use cannabis also smoke tobacco and cannabis is often combined with tobacco in cannabis cigarettes (reference 33, a 2016 review); statistically controlling for tobacco use can potentially remove valuable variance associated with cannabis use, which raises the question of how to balance specificity with generalisability; the same problem holds for ADHD, depression and anxiety. The authors suggest control groups with specific comorbidities and longitudinal extensions of existing studies.

tasks.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Systematic Reviews, 1st paragraph; Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Footnote 1
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Pooled analysis of six case-control studies, four unpublished (2,159 people with lung cancer, 2,985 controls), in the International Lung Cancer Consortium (Zhang et al., 2015): habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking, odds ratio 0.96 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.38); among people who did not smoke tobacco 1.03 (0.51 to 2.08). Habitual means at least 1 joint-year; non-habitual under 1 joint-year, including people who never used cannabis; not smoking tobacco means under 100 cigarettes in a lifetime or the cut-offs of the pooled studies. Adenocarcinoma only: more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75 to 4.00); more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85 to 3.56), described by the pooled analysis's authors as suggestive but not significant. The committee adds that risk rose with duration and intensity, but even people with the heaviest and longest smoking were not at significantly greater risk than people who smoked non-habitually.

tasks.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Primary Literature, 1st paragraph; Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Footnote 2
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Epidemiologic review (Huang et al., 2015; no meta-analysis) of six lung cancer studies, including the pooled analysis and two of its studies. Of the three others, two were set aside by the committee because the pooled analysis's authors described limits (inadequate control of tobacco use, possible reporting bias); the third, a cohort of 49,321 Swedish male military conscripts followed 40 years (44,257 in the cannabis analysis; Callaghan et al., 2013), found a hazard ratio of 2.12 (95% CI 1.08 to 4.14) for more than 50 uses at conscription against never, adjusted for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status at conscription. The committee says the studies in the review but not in the pooled analysis indicate an increased risk. No absolute risks are given. The cohort paper itself was not read.

tasks.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Discussion of Findings, 2nd paragraph
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Limits of the lung cancer evidence as the committee states them: the pooled analysis could not account for differences in smoking technique or in the cannabis smoked, had too few people with heavy long-term smoking for precise estimates, and relied on self-report without biological validation; in the Swedish cohort detailed cannabis and tobacco use before and after baseline was lacking, tobacco and cannabis were not accounted for during the 40-year follow-up, its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco and cannabis, and self-reports were not anonymous.

tasks.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Conclusion 5-1; Chapter Highlights, 1st bullet; Summary, 1st paragraph; Appendix B › Box B-3
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: The committee's graded conclusion 5-1 (quoted here) is its judgment. It rests on the pooled analysis; the cohort and the review are described in the Discussion. Box B-3 defines moderate as several findings from good- to fair-quality studies with very few or no credible opposing findings, where chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out. The Chapter 5 highlight goes further than the numbered conclusion (it says the evidence suggests that smoking cannabis does not increase the risk of lung and head and neck cancer in adults), and the Chapter 5 Summary words the conclusion as no statistically significant association. Beside the numbers, the grade is wider than the pooled interval allows: the interval (0.66 to 1.38) does not exclude a rise, the cohort hazard ratio is 2.12, and the Box B-3 definition asks for very few or no credible opposing findings; the chapter does not explain how these were weighed.

tasks.locator: Appendix B › Literature Search, 1st to 9th paragraphs; Search Strategies (Search 2); Primary Literature: Identification and Quality Review, 3rd paragraph; Data Synthesis and Strength of Evidence Assessment, 1st paragraph; Box B-2; Box B-3; Discussion, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)
tasks.extracted: Method, search: six searches of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (PsycINFO for Search 4) covering January 1999 to 2 August 2016; Searches 2 to 6 were combined into a master library of 10,759 unique articles (1,488 first categorised as systematic reviews), sorted into 11 endpoint areas; filtering to the chosen endpoints left 6,540 primary articles and 288 systematic reviews. The Search 2 listing limits to English-language human studies from 1999. Method, appraisal: possible systematic reviews were screened with six questions, then rated good, fair or poor on five attributes adapted from the Cochrane group by at least two members independently (disagreements settled by deliberation or a third member); only good or fair reviews informed the report. Primary studies were reviewed guided by the Cochrane tool for randomised trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort and case-control studies. The report says the committee was not tasked to conduct a systematic review and that literature may have been missed. Method, wording of conclusions: evidence was privileged in the order randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies, case-control studies, with case series only when nothing better; the committee notes that this order does not imply the size of an observed effect. The weight of evidence was decided in private deliberations of committee subgroups. Box B-3 defines substantial (several supportive findings from good-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings), moderate (several from good- to fair-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings; limitations including chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out), limited (fair-quality studies or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion; significant uncertainty) and no or insufficient (mixed findings, a single poor study, or not studied).

tasks.locator: An Urgent Call for Change in Cannabis Research › Complications of cannabis research, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Tobacco and other co-occurring use: about 70% of people who use cannabis also smoke tobacco and cannabis is often combined with tobacco in cannabis cigarettes (reference 33, a 2016 review); statistically controlling for tobacco use can potentially remove valuable variance associated with cannabis use, which raises the question of how to balance specificity with generalisability; the same problem holds for ADHD, depression and anxiety. The authors suggest control groups with specific comorbidities and longitudinal extensions of existing studies.

tasks.locator: Report Overview › Goal and conclusions, Table 1 (Cancer row)
tasks.extracted: Table 1 sets the report's conclusions beside the WHO report's. Respiratory rows: bronchitis and respiratory symptoms (substantial for increased incidence and severity in people who have smoked cannabis long term; moderate for improvement after cessation), pulmonary function (moderate for acute but not chronic bronchodilatation; moderate for higher lung volume), COPD (limited in people who smoke cannabis occasionally, controlled for tobacco; insufficient for COPD severity), asthma (no or insufficient). Cancer rows: lung and head and neck cancers moderate evidence for no association, against WHO's statement that a cannabis and tobacco mix may increase cancer risk and that the effect of cannabis alone is unknown. Table 1 words the committee's cancer conclusion without the word statistical; the WHO report was not read, so the WHO statement is known only through this table.
